newsitem.title: PERU: Journalists ease tourism damage in Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Journalists ease tourism damage in Peru crisis.

text.p: Hordes of heavy-spending foreign journalists descending on Peru to cover the hostage saga have eased the damage caused to the local tourism industry by the crisis, officials said on Friday.

While international companies think twice before sending their executives to Peru, and travelers cancel their package deals, hundreds of newshounds have been taking their places and packing Lima's major hotels.

"It is true that there have been some cancellations at hotels, especially from businessmen and corporations ... and from Japanese tourists," said Carlos Zuniga, vice president of the National Tourism Chamber.
"However, the arrival of so many journalists has in one way or another compensated these small falls in reservations."

Peru met its target of attracting 600,000 tourists this year a week before heavily armed Marxist guerrillas from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima. They still hold 74 hostages.
This year's recovery, up from 485,000 in 1995, was largely due to the perception that Peru had left its violent past behind -- a perception now shattered by the MRTA.

Although traditionally popular for its archaeological riches, Inca ruins and dramatic Andean and jungle scenery, Peru first lost favour with tourists following the outbreak of a violent guerrilla war in 1980.
A few days into the hostage crisis, the government launched a public relations campaign to convince the world the takeover was an isolated, one-off incident.
Some hardy travelers, cameras in hand, have even added a visit to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence to their travel itinerary.
